content: Tinidazole, when administered at a dose of 600 mg/kg/day in male rats, induced testicular histopathological changes. This dose is approximately three times the highest human therapeutic dose when adjusted for body surface area. Spermatogenic effects were observed at both 300 mg/kg/day and 600 mg/kg/day, with the latter being five times the highest human therapeutic dose based on body surface area conversions. These effects are characteristic of agents within the 5-nitroimidazole class. In acute toxicity studies, the LD50 for mice was generally greater than 3,600 mg/kg for oral administration and greater than 2,300 mg/kg for intraperitoneal administration. In rats, the LD50 was greater than 2,000 mg/kg for both oral and intraperitoneal routes. A repeated-dose toxicology study was conducted in beagle dogs using oral tinidazole at doses of 100 mg/kg/day, 300 mg/kg/day, and 1,000 mg/kg/day for 28 days. On day 18 of the study, the highest dose was reduced to 600 mg/kg/day due to severe clinical symptoms. The compound-related effects observed in the dogs included increased thymus atrophy in both sexes at the middle and high doses, and prostate atrophy in males at all dose levels. A no-adverse-effect level (NOAEL) of 100 mg/kg/day was determined for females, which is nine times the highest human dose based on plasma AUC comparisons. Clinical Studies Trichomoniasis The use of tinidazole (2 g single oral dose) for trichomoniasis has been well-documented in 34 published reports involving over 2,800 patients. In four blinded, randomized, comparative studies assessing efficacy via culture at time points ranging from one week to one month post-treatment, cure rates ranged from 92% (37/40) to 100% (65/65) among 172 total subjects. In four additional blinded, randomized, comparative studies where efficacy was assessed by wet mount between 7–14 days post-treatment, cure rates ranged from 80% (8/10) to 100% (16/16) among 116 total subjects. Tinidazole was found to be superior to placebo and comparable to other anti-trichomonal drugs. In four open-label trials in men, including one comparative study with metronidazole and three single-arm studies, parasitological evaluation of urine preand post-treatment reported cure rates ranging from 83% (25/30) to 100% (80/80) among 142 total subjects. Giardiasis Tinidazole use in giardiasis has been documented in 19 published reports involving over 1,600 patients, including both adults and pediatric populations. In eight controlled studies involving 619 subjects, of whom 299 received a single 2 g dose (or 50 mg/kg in pediatric patients), cure rates ranged from 80% (40/50) to 100% (15/15). In three trials comparing tinidazole to 2–3 days of metronidazole, cure rates for metronidazole ranged from 76% (19/25) to 93% (14/15). Data comparing a single 2 g dose of tinidazole to the usual 5–7 day regimen of metronidazole are limited. Intestinal Amebiasis Tinidazole use in intestinal amebiasis has been documented in 26 published reports involving over 1,400 patients. Most studies utilized a regimen of 2 g/day for three days. In four randomized, controlled studies (one investigator single-blind and three open-label) involving 220 subjects, cure rates after three days of therapy ranged from 86% (25/29) to 93% (25/27). Amebic Liver Abscess Tinidazole use in amebic liver abscess has been documented in 18 published reports involving over 470 patients. Most studies utilized a regimen of 2 g/day for 2–5 days. In seven randomized, controlled studies (one double-blind, one single-blind, and five open-label) involving 133 subjects, cure rates ranged from 81% (17/21) to 100% (16/16). Four of these studies used at least three days of tinidazole therapy. Bacterial Vaginosis A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled clinical trial in 235 non-pregnant women evaluated the efficacy of tinidazole for bacterial vaginosis. Clinical cure required normalization of vaginal discharge and resolution of all Amsel’s criteria, which include (a) homogeneous vaginal discharge, (b) a fishy amine odor when mixed with 10% KOH solution, and (c) the presence of ≥20% clue cells on microscopic examination. Microbiologic diagnosis was based on Gram stain of vaginal smears demonstrating (a) markedly reduced or absent Lactobacillus morphology, (b) predominance of Gardnerella morphotype, and (c) absent or few white blood cells, with quantification of bacterial morphotypes to determine the Nugent score. A score ≥4 was required for study inclusion, and a score of 0–3 was considered a microbiologic cure. Therapeutic cure was defined as a composite endpoint of both clinical and microbiologic cure. Tinidazole oral tablets, administered as either 2 g once daily for two days or 1 g once daily for five days, demonstrated superior efficacy over placebo in achieving therapeutic, clinical, and microbiologic cure. The therapeutic cure rates in this study were based on resolution of all four Amsel’s criteria and a Nugent score of <4. Previous clinical studies with other products approved for bacterial vaginosis used resolution of either two or three out of four Amsel’s criteria as the basis for cure rates.
